# Preface {.unnumbered}

A clinical prediction model is usually reported as a single number: an AUROC of
0.87, say, printed once in an abstract and carried forward as if it described
everyone the model will ever touch. It does not. That number is an average over
a population, and an average is exactly the wrong summary when the question is
whether the model works for the people least represented in the data that built
it.

This is a short, end-to-end walkthrough that builds the standard
model-evaluation toolkit **from scratch**, one estimator at a time, in plain
base R:

- AUROC, as the rank statistic it actually is;
- the calibration slope, and the expected calibration error that so often
  disagrees with it;
- a bootstrap that respects the outcome classes it resamples;
- equalised-odds gaps and per-group thresholds;
- and a power calculation for the subgroup differences everyone reports and
  almost no one is powered to detect.

Nothing is hidden inside a package. Every metric is a few lines you can read,
change, and break, and every one is checked in `R/_test_engine.R` against an
independent reference (`wilcox.test`, `glm`) or against an answer known in
closed form.

::: {.callout-note}
## All data here are simulated

No patient record, cohort, or image dataset is used or shared anywhere in this
project. The simulation is not a shortcut; it is the point. Because the true
AUROC in each subgroup is chosen up front and has a closed form (Φ(d/√2) for
binormal scores with separation *d*), every estimate in these pages can be
judged against the right answer, not against another estimate. You
cannot do that with real data, because with real data you never know the
truth.
:::

## How to read it

The chapters build in order. Chapter 1 shows the headline number and what it
hides. Chapters 2 and 3 set up the three questions any evaluation must answer
and the simulated world we will answer them in. Chapters 4 through 7 build the
tools (discrimination, uncertainty, calibration, thresholds), and Chapter 8 is
a checklist you can take to the next model-evaluation paper you read.

The fastest way to understand any of it is to break the simulation on purpose.
Open `R/simulate.R`, change the separation `d` in one stratum, or shrink an `n`
until the interval swallows the effect, and re-render. The estimators will tell
you what you did.

## Running the code

```bash
Rscript R/_test_engine.R   # validate every estimator against its reference
Rscript R/make_results.R   # regenerate every number in the book
quarto render              # build the site into docs/
```

The estimators are pure base R with no package dependencies; `ggplot2` is used
only to draw the figures.
